requested.title: Unvalidated WebSocket frames are persisted into the replayed history and crash every client's parser
Client-asserted `userId` is relayed unvalidated, enabling message impersonation
No Origin check on the WebSocket upgrade (cross-site WebSocket hijacking)
Rate-limit verdict read across an `await` from hitlimit's shared, mutated result object
Unauthenticated email-send actions have no rate limit and flush a shared global outbox
Unauthenticated /sse/time and /ws/time allocate an unbounded per-connection 1s timer that cannot be rate-limited or timed out
Module-scope WeakMap loses interval handles across dev hot-reload, leaking a 1s timer per pre-reload socket
@defaultSensitive=false inverts varlock's fail-closed secret default for a schema whose values are rendered on a public page
Lazy init memoizes only the resolved value, so concurrent requests each run a full varlock load() — and a failing load() re-runs forever
load() runs inside a request handler and patchGlobalConsole() is never called on the real site, contradicting both the published example and the page's own copy
Reads varlock's internal __VARLOCK_ENV transport instead of its public API; unguarded JSON.parse 500s on encrypted or frozen-env deployments

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: The mechanism is confirmed. `message` (routes.ts:47-70) checks only byte length (L49) and text-ness (L53), then pushes the raw frame into `history` (L63) and rebroadcasts it (L68-69); nothing validates the `{userId, text}` envelope. `open` (L41-46) replays every entry to each new socket, and ChatWidget.svelte:52-55 does a bare `JSON.parse(e.data)` then dereferences `msg.text`/`msg.userId` with no try/catch, so `boom` throws SyntaxError and `null` throws TypeError in every receiving browser. I verified there is no XSS: the template renders `{msg.text}` (escaped by Svelte, no `{@html}`). I am downgrading severity because two of the finding's impact claims overstate reality. First, an exception inside an `addEventListener` callback does not remove the listener or break the socket — subsequent valid frames still render, so there is no persistent 'parser crash', only one console error per bad frame. Second, the poisoning is not permanent: `history` is FIFO-bounded to 100 entries / 64 KB (L65-67), so garbage is evicted by ordinary traffic, and a process restart clears it. The net harm is therefore console noise plus blank bubbles occupying history slots on a public demo widget — a real missing-input-validation defect at a trust boundary the server is positioned to enforce (and the same class the maintainers already fixed for this file in #332/#347), but no confidentiality or meaningful integrity impact, so BUG rather than a security MEDIUM. The recommended fix (parse in try/catch, require a bounded `{userId, text}`, store and broadcast the canonical re-serialized form) is correct.

The code description is accurate — the client mints a UUID into localStorage (ChatWidget.svelte:28-34), sends it in every envelope (L84), the server relays it untouched (routes.ts:63-69), and each receiver computes ownership with `msg.userId === userId` (L54) — but there is no security boundary here to cross. I traced every consumer of `userId` in the widget: its only effect is `class:mine` on the message row (L102), i.e. whether a bubble is right-aligned and accent-coloured. There is no author label rendered anywhere, no account, no session, no privilege, and no server-side authorization that reads the field; `upgrade()`'s `rateKey` is used solely for the rate-limit bucket and deliberately is not an identity. So 'impersonation' amounts to making a bubble appear right-aligned in one victim's viewport — attacker-chosen CSS alignment, not attribution of authorship to anyone. The claimed disclosure is likewise empty: the UUID is an anonymous, self-assigned, meaningless-outside-this-chat token that grants nothing when harvested, and broadcasting it is structurally required by the demo's design (client-side `fromMe` computation in a dumb relay). This is precisely the 'demonstration code … no auth' class the project documents as a known false positive, and unlike F1/F3 there is no resource bound or cross-origin control missing. The recommendation (mint identity in `upgrade()`, keep it on `ws.data.user`, echo the connection's own id on open) is sound design advice for anyone copying the pattern into a real app, but it fixes no exploitable flaw here.

Every link in the chain checks out. `KIND_POLICY` in runtime/requestSetup.ts:66 sets `ws: { csrf: false, ... }`, so `csrfCheck` is skipped for every ws route (requestSetup.ts:119-126 is gated on `policy.csrf`); `Mochi.ws<T>(handlers)` (Mochi.ts:227-236) accepts no config object at all, so there is no `csrf` or `rateLimit` option; and Mochi.ts:1290-1305 shows `upgrade()` returning `false` is the only available rejection path — the chat's `upgrade` (routes.ts:38-40) only derives a rate key and never reads `Origin`. Bun's `server.upgrade()` performs no origin validation. WebSocket handshakes are not subject to the same-origin policy and are not preflighted, so any third-party page a visitor loads can open `wss://mochi.fast/ws/chat`, receive the replayed history, and write into the shared buffer from the victim's IP. The concrete security consequence is the one the finding names: `rateKeyFor()` keys the 20-messages/10s window on `getClientAddress()`, which behind the site's nginx (`proxy: { addressHeader: 'x-forwarded-for', xffDepth: 1 }`) resolves to the real visitor IP — so distributing writes across drive-by visitors defeats the only control on the buffer, and the content is attributed to victims' addresses upstream. I am keeping MEDIUM: this is a missing cross-origin control (CWE-1385) that bypasses another security control, and #349's own commit message states that `upgrade` 'is exactly where auth and client identity belong', confirming the hook exists and is simply unused. I note the classic CSWSH harm — cross-origin reading of cookie-authenticated data — does not apply, since the socket carries no session and the history is already public, which is why this is MEDIUM and not higher.

The code pattern is exactly as described, but the interleaving it requires cannot occur on this codebase's Bun. Confirmed facts: `rateLimitMemoryStore()` returns hitlimit's `MemoryStore` unwrapped (rateLimit.ts:123-125); `MemoryStore.hit()` is synchronous and returns `this._result`, a single object allocated once per store and overwritten on every call (dist/index.js:8, 40-48); and `const { count } = await limiter.hit(...)` reads it one microtask after the call. Two things kill exploitability. (1) Store isolation: the chat's `limiter` is a dedicated instance created at module scope (routes.ts:31), and I grepped the whole repo — routes.ts:57 is the only `.hit()` call against it. Every framework limiter allocates its own store (`options.store ?? rateLimitMemoryStore()`, rateLimit.ts:207), so no HTTP route, no other demo, and no framework `checkLimit` path can touch this `_result`. The only possible interleaving is chat-message-to-chat-message. (2) Bun's event loop forecloses that: the Bun v1.0.26 release notes state 'we've made some infrastructure tweaks to ensure that microtasks are always drained after event loop callbacks are executed. There was a bug where we skipped doing this in websockets…'. This repo pins Bun 1.4.4 (.bun-version, Dockerfile ARG BUN_IMAGE), far past that fix, so the resumption microtask that reads `_result` runs to completion before any other websocket callback can invoke `hit()` again. Mochi's dispatcher (Mochi.ts:1996) discards the handler's promise, but that only means it does not await — it does not let two callbacks share one drain window. Neither the bypass nor the over-block case is reachable. The latent shared-mutable-return hazard is genuine and the suggested snapshot/wrapper fix remains worthwhile defensive hygiene (it would matter if a future store were truly async or shared across routes), which is why I note BUG rather than dismissing it outright — but there is no rate-limit bypass today.

The missing control is real and verified end-to-end. The page declares no `rateLimit` and packages/site/src/index.ts passes none to `Mochi.serve()`, so `buildLimiter(undefined, pattern)` returns null (Mochi.ts:801-828) and `checkRouteLimit` (Mochi.ts:981) is a no-op; I confirmed `wrapRequest` wraps the POST action handler too (Mochi.ts:1026-1027), so a page-level `rateLimit` with `skip: (req) => req.method !== 'POST'` would in fact gate these actions — exactly the idiom already applied to `/demos/queue` and `/demos/reload-form-data` (both `limit: 60, window: '1m'`) by commit 1289d8f8, plus 60/m on captcha mint and 120/m on `/og`. So this is a clean, inconsistent gap in a control the maintainers demonstrably treat as required. The per-request work is as described: `sendEmail` → `renderEmailComponent` does a `renderStatic` SSR render, joins scoped CSS, runs `@css-inline/css-inline-wasm` `inline()`, then an `HTMLRewriter` pass and `htmlToText` (email/render.ts, mailer.ts:89-95); `sendPhoto` re-reads the JPEG from disk every request (routes.ts:26) and the bytes are retained in the outbox entry (devOutbox.ts:70-74). I also confirmed the deployed site really is in dev mode — Dockerfile's ENTRYPOINT is `bun run dev:${WORKSPACE}` and packages/site's `dev` script sets `NODE_ENV=development` — so the transport is `dev` (email/config.ts:12), the capture target is the shared process-global outbox capped at `MAX_OUTBOX = 100`, and CSRF only warns in development, making the POST reachable with no Origin at all. I am downgrading from MEDIUM because the amplification is modest rather than asymmetric: every ordinary page on this site is an unlimited unauthenticated SSR render, so the marginal cost here is roughly a CSS-inline pass and a page-cached 32 KB read; no mail is ever delivered (recipient, subject, body and attachment are all fixed server-side and the transport never sends); and the one distinctive effect, evicting other visitors' captures from the bounded dev outbox, degrades only a dev-only viewer. Real defect, correct fix, non-security-grade impact.

All three framework claims are confirmed by source. (1) `checkRouteLimit` is called in exactly two places — Mochi.ts:981 (page) and Mochi.ts:1211 (api); the ws branch (Mochi.ts:1258+) and sse branch (Mochi.ts:1332+) never call it, and `resolveLimiter` is likewise only invoked in the page/api registration branches, so the global `rateLimit` serve option cannot reach these routes either. `Mochi.ws(handlers)` and `Mochi.sse(handler)` (Mochi.ts:227-236) take no config, unlike `page`/`api` which accept `{ rateLimit }`. (2) Neither branch invokes `middleware`, so no `sequence()` handle can gate them — the site's whole `handle` chain is bypassed. (3) `KIND_POLICY.sse.timeout === true` (requestSetup.ts:65) runs `server.timeout(req, 0)` (requestSetup.ts:85-87); the framework's own docs confirm the intent — 'Mochi already disables the idle timer for page renders and SSE streams' (packages/docs/160-serve-options.md:128). I also verified `MochiSseStream.send` calls `controller.enqueue(frame)` unconditionally with no `desiredSize` check (Mochi.ts:1398), and the stream is constructed with the default count-based queuing strategy, so a client that holds the connection open without reading grows the per-stream queue without bound while the disabled idle timer guarantees the socket never expires; `/ws/time` has the same shape via `ws.send` with no return-value check and no `drain`, and `websocket: { idleTimeout: 30 }` cannot help because the server writes every second. Unlike F5's per-request CPU, these are persistent per-connection resources — one 1 Hz timer, one never-expiring socket and one monotonically growing queue each — with no cap at any layer and no route-level knob to add one, which is the same 'unbounded resource growth on public demo routes' class commit 1289d8f8 treated as a security fix for the chat and HN caches. MEDIUM stands. The recommendations (a module-scope connection ceiling keyed on `getClientAddress()`, 503 before constructing the stream, `upgrade()` returning false for ws, and a `desiredSize` check in `MochiSseStream.send`) are all sound; note `upgrade` is confirmed to be the one callback with a working `getRequestContext()` (Mochi.ts:1294-1297).

Confirmed in full. `intervals` is a `WeakMap` created inside the IIFE at routes.ts:7, so it belongs to one module evaluation. On a dev reload, devWatcher rebuilds the entry and calls `extractServeOptions(outFile, { fresh: true })` (devWatcher.ts:340), re-evaluating the whole first-party graph — a brand-new empty WeakMap and new closures — then hot-swaps via `wsHandlersMap.set(pattern, handler.handlers)` (devWatcher.ts:517). Mochi's Bun `close` handler reads the live map at dispatch time: `wsHandlersMap.get(ws.data.__mochiRoutePattern)?.close?.(ws, code, reason)` (Mochi.ts:2004), so a socket opened before the reload — whose handle lives only in the discarded WeakMap — hits `clearInterval(intervals.get(ws))` with `undefined`, a silent no-op. I also verified the framework passes Bun's `ServerWebSocket` straight through to `open`/`close` without wrapping, so the WeakMap keying is correct in the steady state and only the reload boundary breaks it, exactly as the finding states. The orphaned interval's closure holds `ws` strongly, so neither the timer nor the socket can be collected, and it keeps calling `ws.send` on a dead socket once a second for the life of the process. This fires on essentially every save with the demo tab open, because `applyRouteChanges` swaps the handlers before the browser is told to reload and close its socket. Notably the framework documents this exact hazard class — packages/docs/170-development-mode.md warns that each reload re-creates module-scoped singletons holding an OS resource (it names `setInterval` specifically) and prescribes `pinGlobal`, with a `recompile:module-churn` event firing after ten reloads — so this demo simply does not follow the project's own guidance. Dev-only, self-limited to one dev session, hence BUG; the recommended fixes (stash the handle on `ws.data.user` via an `upgrade` handler, or `pinGlobal` the map as lib/highlight.server.ts does) are both correct.

The varlock internals are reported accurately — `ConfigItem._isSensitive = true` is the class default (env-graph-D-UUzmAA.mjs:5884), `resolveSensitiveSource()` consults `@defaultSensitive` only when the data type has no opinion (L5978-6043), `EnvGraph.overrideValues = originalProcessEnv` in the constructor (L8820) with `isOverridden` resolving a declared key from it (L5662, L5677), and env.ts:40-45 does publish every graph entry gated solely on `item.isSensitive`. But the exposure the finding infers does not exist. First I checked the base data types: `DataType.isSensitive` returns `def.sensitive` (env-source-fingerprint-DPQ2KgPB.mjs:47-49) and no built-in type declares it, so without `@defaultSensitive=false` all four keys would inherit the fail-closed `true` and the demo's entire table would render as masked bullets — the header is the mechanism that makes this demo function, not a security regression, and marking the three keys `@public` instead is a pure style change with identical behaviour. Second, the claimed read-back channel into the deployed environment is closed: only schema-declared keys exist in `configSchema`, `overrideValues` is consulted per-declared-item, and I confirmed there is no `.env`/`.env.local` anywhere under packages/site (the only env file in the whole package is this schema), so the renderable set is permanently the four hardcoded `DEMO_*` names — none of which the production process sets, and all of which are placeholder values committed to git. An attacker cannot introduce a key, because the schema is a static file in the image. Third, the one genuinely sensitive key is explicitly `@sensitive` and is masked, which the finding itself concedes. What remains is 'a future maintainer might add a key and forget `@sensitive`' — a hardening suggestion about demo documentation, not a present defect — which lands squarely in the project's documented 'judge packages/site/src/demos/* as documentation, not product' rule. The defence-in-depth recommendation (project an explicit allowlist in `loadVarlockConfig`) is reasonable but fixes nothing exploitable.

The code defect is exactly as described and I confirmed it line by line: `cached` is assigned only at env.ts:47, after `await load()` at L34, while the guard reads it at L30 — so there is no in-flight promise to join and no negative caching. Every request arriving inside the first load's window starts its own `load()`, and `load()` is genuinely heavy and side-effecting: `loadVarlockEnvGraph()` → `loadEnvGraph()` constructs a disk-backed `CacheStore`, probes the local-encrypt backend, parses and resolves the graph, then `load()` writes `process.env.__VARLOCK_ENV` and calls `initVarlockEnv()`, which deletes previously-injected keys and rewrites `envState.originalProcessEnv` back over `process.env` (env-CeXQINKg.mjs:547-556). The error half is the substantive part and it is correct: `checkForSchemaErrors`/`checkForConfigErrors` throw, `cached` stays null forever, and every subsequent request re-runs the whole load and re-prints the per-item error block to stderr — an unauthenticated, unbounded retry-and-log loop on a public page with no self-limiting, reachable if a deployed environment ever sets `DEMO_SECRET_KEY` to something not matching `startsWith=sk-` or `DEMO_APP_ENV` outside the enum (both resolve from `process.env` via `overrideValues`), or on any transient load failure. Two corrections that do not change the verdict: `initVarlockEnv()` is fully synchronous, so concurrent loads cannot interleave *inside* it and each rewrite is atomic and idempotent — 'interleaved in attacker-controlled order' overstates the hazard to repeated identical rewrites; and the duplicate-load window only exists before the first success, so the concurrency half is a brief thundering herd rather than a standing exposure. BUG is the right severity, and memoizing the promise with an explicit failure policy is the correct fix.

The factual observations are all verifiable — packages/site/src/index.ts contains zero varlock references (I read it end to end), the only entry is routes.ts:7 → `serverProps` → `loadVarlockConfig()` → `await load()` at env.ts:34, and the demo's own index.ts does `await load(); patchGlobalConsole();` before `Mochi.serve()` — but neither the 'contradiction' nor the security consequence holds up. On the contradiction: a demo's `index.ts` tab is an illustrative file across this entire codebase, never the real entry. CLAUDE.md makes that an explicit rule ('Demos must reference this file (labelled as index.ts), never the real ./src/index.ts — the real one carries site-wide middleware/branding that would obscure the demo'), so the divergence is the documented convention for every demo, not a defect in this one. The page copy also does not claim the site boots this way: it says 'These values were parsed, coerced, and validated by varlock during this page's SSR render', which is precisely what happens, and the `patchGlobalConsole()` sentence is describing what the index.ts tab teaches. At most the intro prose ('you load() the schema once at boot') is loose for a demo that loads lazily — a wording nit in marketing copy, not a code defect. On the security consequence: the finding concedes the only `@sensitive` value is the committed placeholder `sk-demo-000000000000`, so the absent `patchGlobalConsole()` redacts nothing real and the `process.env` injection plants four `DEMO_*` placeholders that nothing in the site reads. The genuinely questionable behaviour the finding brushes against — a public GET rewriting the long-lived server's `process.env` on the second and later `initVarlockEnv()` call, which restores `originalProcessEnv` wholesale and would clobber any post-boot mutation — is only reachable via the missing memoization, i.e. it is F9's defect, already credited there. Nothing here is independently real and exploitable.

The premise that `__VARLOCK_ENV` is an internal transport that is 'not always JSON' is correct, and varlock does prefix-check before parsing (env-CeXQINKg.mjs:517-521), but the specific failure the finding predicts is unreachable here because of call ordering. I read `load()` in full (dist/index.mjs:11-19): it is linear and its second-to-last statement is `process.env.__VARLOCK_ENV = JSON.stringify(envGraph.getSerializedGraph())`, executed *before* `initVarlockEnv()`. So whatever the variable held on entry — a `varlock:v1:` ciphertext under `@encryptInjectedEnv`, or an injected blob from a `varlock freeze` / `_VARLOCK_USE_INJECTED_ENV=1` parent — is unconditionally overwritten with plain JSON by the time env.ts:36 reads it. I verified `getSerializedGraph()` returns an object literal (`{ blobFormatVersion: 1, varlockVersion, basePath, sources, config, settings }`, env-graph-D-UUzmAA.mjs:9252-9260), so its `JSON.stringify` always begins with `{` and can never carry the encrypted prefix. The early-return path the finding cites (`if (opts?.allowFail || globalThis.__varlockEnvReady) return`) leaves the blob untouched, but that blob is already the JSON this code then parses successfully — and `load()` passes no `opts`, so the only way to reach that branch is with a prefix that `load()` has just removed. There is therefore no unhandled `SyntaxError` and no 500 from this line; if anything upstream fails, `load()` itself throws and L36 never runs (which is F9's territory). The secondary claim — that a future `blobFormatVersion` shape drift would silently render a blank table via `graph.config ?? {}` — is hypothetical fragility about an unreleased version, not a current bug. Reading an internal transport instead of the typed `ENV` proxy or `internal.*` accessors is a legitimate robustness/style criticism and the guards suggested are cheap, but no defect is present today.
